embeds.title: HOW PSBL SCORING WORKS
embeds.description: The PSBL scoring system has two goals: points should reward what a player does well, and every lineup slot should matter about as much as its share of your lineup. Each value was tested against every MLB player's 2024, 2025 and 2026 regular seasons, about 2,250 hitter seasons and 2,600 pitcher seasons, and the reasons are below.

fields.name: HITTERS
fields.value:
Single **+1**
Double **+2**
Triple **+3**
Home Run **+4**
Run **+1** • RBI **+1**
Walk **+1** • Hit by Pitch **+1**
Stolen Base **+2** • Caught Stealing **−1**
Strikeout **−0.5**

fields.name: PITCHERS
fields.value:
Inning Pitched **+3** (+1 per out)
Strikeout **+1.25**
Hit, Walk or Hit Batter **−1** each
Earned Run **−2**
Win **+2** • Loss **−1**
Save **+6** • Hold **+4**

fields.name: **━━━ HITTING ━━━**
fields.value:
**Familiar on purpose.** Total bases, runs, RBI and walks are the stats every owner already knows. Across the three seasons they split a hitter's points about evenly: singles, home runs, runs and RBI each about a fifth, walks about a seventh and steals about a twentieth. Power, on-base skill and speed each have a real path to value, and no single stat carries a hitter.

Steals stay at 2. At 1.5, a hitter's points repeated less well from one season to the next, so the cut would have made results noisier without making them fairer.

fields.name: **━━━ STARTING PITCHERS ━━━**
fields.value:
**Paid for outs and strikeouts, charged for baserunners and runs.** An average MLB start in these seasons scored about **11 points**. An everyday hitter averaged about **2.6 points a game**, so over a week a starter's slot and a hitter's slot come out close: about 406 points a season for a league's 60 starting pitchers against 424 for its 120 starting hitters.

Strikeouts are the most repeatable thing a pitcher does. At **1.25**, starters' points repeat better from season to season than at any lower value tested (a correlation of 0.54, against 0.45 under typical redraft values).

fields.name: **━━━ WINS AND SAVES ━━━**
fields.value:
**Counted, but kept small.** A win depends on the offense and the bullpen, so it's worth **+2** and a loss **−1**: about 2% of pitcher points, against about 8% when a win is worth 7.

Saves (**+6**) and holds (**+4**) make relievers worth a roster spot without letting closers swamp the board. With a 7-point save and no holds, 4 to 6 relievers ranked among the 25 most valuable players each season; here it's 0 to 3. Holds give setup men value, so your three RP slots aren't only a closer hunt.

fields.name: WHAT A GAME CAN LOOK LIKE
fields.value:
Homer, single, walk, 2 runs, 3 RBI, a strikeout → **+10.5**
0 for 4 with 2 strikeouts → **−1.0**
6 IP, 5 H, 2 ER, 1 BB, 7 K, win → **+18.75**
4 IP, 8 H, 6 ER, 3 BB, 3 K, loss → **−8.25**
Closer: 1 IP, 1 H, 2 K, save → **+10.5**
Setup man: 1 IP, 1 K, hold → **+8.25**

fields.name: **━━━ WHAT ISN'T SCORED ━━━**
fields.value:
**Quality starts:** innings and earned runs already reward a long, clean start, so a bonus would count it twice.
**Complete games, shutouts and no-hitters:** the same reason.
**Blown saves:** the hits, runs and any loss already cost him.
**Grand slams, cycles and walk-offs:** those hits and RBI already count; a bonus mostly rewards luck.

fields.name: **━━━ FOR YOUR ROSTER ━━━**
fields.value: Over a season, hitters score about **58%** of a team's points, starters about **28%** and relievers about **15%**, close to their share of the 18 lineup slots (56%, 28% and 17%). The best seasons from 2024 to 2026 scored about 700 to 795 for a hitter, 630 to 650 for a starter and 500 to 530 for a reliever. Half and quarter points make an exact weekly tie very rare.
